notes:
I've put notes on 1 Samuel 24 together below. I didn't find any Lutheran, Orthodox or modern-scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) commentary on this chapter, or any prosperity or hyper-grace material, so those parts are left out. I couldn't open Wesley's own notes either; for the Methodist view I've used Adam Clarke, whom StudyLight labels Wesleyan/Methodist. David Guzik (Enduring Word) is on your Pentecostal/charismatic site list, though his sources don't call him Pentecostal.

**v. 1**
- In chapter 23, God saved David by drawing Saul away to fight the Philistines just as Saul was ready to catch him, according to Guzik (Spanish edition). https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/1-de-samuel-24/
- Ellicott (Anglican) says Saul set off again as soon as the Philistine raid was over, which shows how set he was on killing David. He thinks the Ziphites from chapter 23 helped guide him. Ellicott describes En-gedi as an oasis whose limestone cliffs have many large caves, big enough to hide a lot of men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says David boldly crossed the desert because the Ziphites kept watching him on the western side. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-24.html

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: sending 3,000 hand-picked men shows Saul treated David as a rival king. "Rocks of the Wild Goats" probably means ibex rocks, and ibex still live there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott on sheepfolds: they were stone walls built across cave mouths. From deep inside a dark cave you can see the entrance clearly, but someone coming in from daylight can't see in.
- **Different readings of "went in to relieve himself"** (KJV "to cover his feet"):
  - Ellicott takes it to mean Saul went in to sleep, following the Syriac Peshitta and Ewald. He argues the usual reading doesn't fit, because David needed time to be told, creep up, cut the robe and get back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
  - Gill also thinks Saul was probably asleep. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-4.html
  - Guzik keeps the usual reading and suggests Saul may have put his robe down in one part of the cave while he went to another. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/
  - Coffman reports that Both Young and Keil expressed the opinion that, upon his entry into the cave, Saul laid his robe aside. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-samuel-24.html

**v. 4**
- **Did God really say this?**
  - Constable: There is no record in the text that God had indeed told David what they said He had. God may have promised David victory, but He never gave permission to kill His anointed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-24.html
  - Ellicott: this was the men's own version of known promises (1 Sam 15:28; 16:1, 12; 20:15; 23:17). He adds that a prophet such as Gad might also have spoken publicly about David's future. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
  - Ligonier (Reformed) agrees that God never told David to assassinate Saul, so the kingdom would have come to him by wrong means. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/david-spares-sauls-life
- Guzik: David's men saw the moment as a gift from God. David refused to fulfil God's promise by disobeying God, because removing Saul was God's job. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/
- Clarke (Methodist): David seems to have got up meaning to kill Saul, but his conscience stopped him, and he cut the robe only to show Saul he could have killed him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-4.html
- Ellicott pictures David tempted for a moment and then stopping, struck that Saul was the Lord's anointed. He sees here David's lasting loyalty to Saul's family, shown later when he pardoned Mephibosheth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm

**v. 5: why was David's conscience troubled? Commentators differ**
- Ellicott: not because of the robe. He was troubled by the brief thought of killing the Lord's anointed. Ellicott sees no sign that David regretted cutting the hem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
- Gill: David saw cutting the robe itself as a great insult to his king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-5.html
- Matthew Henry (Presbyterian): the act did Saul no real harm, but David repented because it was an affront. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-5.html
- Geneva Bible notes (Reformed): For seeing it was his own private cause, he repented that he had touched his enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/24-5.htm
- Constable: by cutting the robe, David hinted he could cut off Saul's reign just as easily. His act constituted mild rebellion against Saul's authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-5.html
- The Biblical Illustrator draws the lesson of listening to conscience even in small things. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tbi/1-samuel-24.html
- Ellicott also reports a Babylonian Talmud saying that strongly condemns cutting the robe, linking it to old David finding no warmth in his clothes (1 Kings 1:1). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm

**v. 6: "the LORD's anointed"**
- Ligonier: David stayed his hand not because Saul deserved to live but because he was not Saul's appointed judge. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/david-spares-sauls-life
- Ligonier, a separate article: David accepted that Saul, though unworthy, held a role God had given him. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/do-not-touch-the-lords-anointed
- **Catholic (Augustine, writing against the Donatists):**
  - Saul and David received the same outward anointing. What differed was not "the sacrament" but personal merit. Augustine asks what David honoured in Saul, if not the holiness of the sacrament. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/14092.htm
  - In *City of God*, he says Saul's anointing is to be taken as a "great mystery" that David honoured so much he trembled over cutting the robe. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf102.iv.XVII.6.html
- **Debated popular teaching ("touch not the Lord's anointed" used to shield leaders):**
  - Ligonier: many evangelicals take this verse to mean pastors cannot be questioned or criticised, and the article rejects that. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/do-not-touch-the-lords-anointed
  - Conrad Mbewe (TGC Africa): the phrase is about harm, especially physical harm. It isn't about legitimate criticism. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/touch-not-the-lords-anointed/
  - Stephen Braimah (TGC Africa): David even used this incident to rebuke Saul. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/who-is-anointed-by-god-what-does-it-mean/
  - Guzik: it is entirely wrong for people to use the idea of touch not the Lord's anointed to insulate a leader from all evaluation or accountability. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/
  - A Bible Hub study note leans the other way, saying "touch" covers every form of mistreatment—from subtle slander to outright violence. https://biblehub.com/psalms/105-15.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew for "restrained" is forceful, literally "crushed down". David held his men back only with some effort. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
- Guzik: David didn't leave Saul for his men to kill. Seeing David's godliness held them back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: David's words and deep bow were the highest honour an inferior could give, to show he was no rival king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
- Guzik: bowing left David completely exposed, which showed great trust in God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the slanderers at court included Doeg, Cush the Benjamite (Psalm 7's heading) and the Ziphites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
- Guzik: David tactfully blamed "men" rather than Saul, covering Saul's shame. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/

**v. 10**
- Ellicott on the text: literally it reads as if the LORD "bade [me] kill thee", but he says that goes against the whole story. The KJV follows the Syriac and Aramaic by adding "some". The Vulgate reads "I thought to kill thee". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
- Precept Austin sees two reasons David gives: he pitied Saul, and Saul was the LORD's anointed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-24-commentary
- Matthew Henry: David turns his men's urging into evidence, because if he had listened to such men Saul would be dead. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_024.cfm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: "my father" is not "father-in-law". It is the respect of a younger man and a loyal subject. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch see childlike reverence for the Lord's anointed in the words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/24-11.htm
- Matthew Henry: the robe is undeniable proof against the charge, since David could have had Saul's head instead. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-11.html
- Guzik: the cut robe recalls Samuel's torn robe in 1 Samuel 15:27-28. Through it God was telling Saul his royal authority was being cut away. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/
- Constable: the chapter turns on "cutting off". David could have cut off Saul's life, cut off only the hem, and finally promised not to cut off Saul's descendants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-24.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik: David handed the case to the LORD, and proved his promise by not killing Saul. He cites the Living Bible's paraphrase, in which God might kill Saul but David never would. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/
- Ligonier: David was content to let God punish Saul in God's time, because vengeance belongs to the Lord. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-spares-sauls-life

**v. 13**
- Ellicott quotes Clericus and Grotius: actions match the heart, so a plotter would have used this chance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/24.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: deeds test principles, so sparing Saul came from a righteous heart. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-24.html

**v. 14**
- Keil and Delitzsch: David meant he was a perfectly harmless and insignificant man, of whom Saul had no occasion to be afraid.
- Clarke: "dead dog" was a Hebrew expression of the deepest contempt.
- Gill: a flea is hard to catch and worthless once caught, a picture of David always on the move.
- Constable: the comparisons may also have warned Saul not to think David helpless.
- All four: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-14.html
- Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew says "one flea". David means a king shouldn't go out with 3,000 men to hunt a single flea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/24-14.htm
- Older critical view: Cheyne thought "a single flea" absurd and proposed changing the text to "wild ass of the desert". https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Flea

**v. 15**
- Guzik: rather than escape his trial by his own effort, David did the harder thing and trusted God to rescue him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/

**vv. 16–19**
- Guzik: Saul seems sincere; his heart melted under David's "coals of kindness". https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_1Sa/1Sa_24.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: David's patience also tested Saul, and shows God's mercy still lingering over him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-24.html
- Ligonier calls it one of Saul's "lucid moments". https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-spares-sauls-life
- Matthew Henry on v. 19: Saul admits no one would spare an enemy like this, then hands David over to God for his reward, either unable or unwilling to repay him himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_024.cfm

**vv. 20–21**
- Constable: David had already made this promise to Jonathan (1 Sam 20:14-17). To "cut off a name" meant to wipe out someone's memory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-24.html
- Matthew Henry: Saul, who had ruined his own soul without repenting, still worried about his name. He wanted David's oath because he knew David kept his word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_024.cfm
- Kelly: the guilty king is now the one afraid. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-5.html

**v. 22**
- Bridgeway: Saul, however, gave no promise to spare David. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-5.html
- Guzik: David stayed in the stronghold because real repentance shows in the lasting direction of a life, not in one emotional moment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-24/
- Ligonier: it was only a short break, since Saul soon chased David again (ch. 26). https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/david-spares-saul-again
- Constable: chapters 24 and 26 mirror each other. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-24.html
